sections.note: This course will discuss issues related to Indigenous sovereignty from an Indigenous hemispheric perspective, especially the critical and historical aspects of contemporary Indigenous intellectual projects, struggles, and demands. This course reflects aspects of Indigenous movements, human rights, and racial formations across the hemisphere (Turtle Island and Abiayala).

AIS 285: Who or what is an Indigenous Thinker? This course seeks to introduce you to a wide range of Indigenous theorists or what we are calling thinkers. This is an Indigenous Thinkers course is devoted to understanding Native American and Indigenous environmental issues in the United States and Canada. We will explore the unique knowledge, practices, and perspectives of Thinkers/Theorists primarily Native American and Indigenous peoples regarding numerous environmental issues such as relationships, land/water, methods, sovereignty, and climate change. Not all the theorists/thinkers will be Indigenous but they will all engage with Indigenous studies and this course prioritizes Indigenous perspectives.

In this course we will learn from Indigenous ways of knowing and thinking and engage with the critical insights unique to Indigenous Studies scholarship. We will explore the historical and cultural depth of Indigenous intellectual traditions as we study critical Indigenous theory’s interventions into settler colonial logics and practices. The books we study will address key areas of focus in Indigenous Studies such as settler colonialism; feminist and queer theory; ethics of relationality and kinship; ecocriticism and environmental studies; literature and story; sovereignty and political order; and law. We will engage in a practice of listening and learning from Indigenous scholars and consider how Indigenous Studies compels us to reflect on the knowledge institutions and learning practices with which we are familiar.

AIS 503: Seminar in Indigenous Studies: Indigenous Geographies: This class will look at space and place from Indigenous geographical thought and the relations Tribal Nations have with their ancestral homelands and environment. This class will privilege Indigenous Geographies from the Great Lakes region and the Midwest, but will also include readings from Canada and Latin America. Indigenous Geographies will also give attention to the impacts and disruptions from settler colonialism, while uplifting Tribal Nations self-determination and contemporary efforts to restore their homelands.
